newsitem.title: UK: Microprocessors still powering ahead after 25 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Microprocessors still powering ahead after 25 yrs.

text.p: Microprocessors, the brains of computers, will only improve with age, Intel Corp. said on Friday at a press conference celebrating the 25th anniversary of their invention.
Using silicon wafers with integrated transistors, microprocessors will continue to steadily increase in power while getting smaller and cheaper, Intel said.
"If current industry trends continue, microprocessors will become tenfold faster and more powerful than they are today, facilitating an endless array of new applications," Intel said in a statement.
The microprocessor has come a long way since 1971, when Intel's first computer chips contained the equivalent of only two transistors.
Since then, the number of transistors has doubled about every two years, with each chip now containing 10,000 transistors. By 2000, each chip is expected to contain 100,000 transistors.
This explosive growth has helped slash the cost of a personal computer from about $6,200 in 1991 to $1,400 in 1995.
Meanwhile, the cost of a chip's data has shrunk from the equivalent of $225 for each million instructions per second to only $11.

Cheaper, more powerful microprocessors have found their way into a huge range of everyday uses, including electronic games and appliances, car engine systems, traffic light controllers, musical instruments, cellular telephones and cash registers.
As microprocessors evolve, they will vastly improve consumer access to the worlds of entertainment and communications.

"At home, people will be able to view and print family photos from digital cameras. The increase in power will make them easier to use, allow voice and handwriting recognition and life-like animation," said Keith Chapple, managing director of Intel Corp. U.K.
In addition, "audio, video and conferencing capabilities will be integrated with the World Wide Web" and the Internet, he said.
